title: Heel Pain with Prior Ankle Fracture - Post-traumatic Osteoarthritis
patient_instructions: You are Anthony Barnes, a 58-year-old storeman. You have had aching pain in and around your right heel/hindfoot for several months, gradually worsening. It is worse the more you walk or stand and eases with rest; it aches deep in the heel and the back of the foot. If asked: you fractured your right ankle badly about 6 years ago (needed a cast, possibly surgery) and the ankle has never felt quite the same since - it feels stiff and your heel looks a bit wider than the other side. You have some morning stiffness in the ankle that eases within about 20-30 minutes. There is NO sharp first-step pain under the heel that is classic for the sole (or only mildly), no numbness or pins and needles, no calf pain or swelling, no fevers, no weight loss, no night pain waking you. No other joints affected. Your ideas: you think the old injury is 'catching up' with you. Your concerns: you are worried you will not be able to keep working on your feet. Your expectation: pain relief and to know what is wrong. You are matter-of-fact. If the candidate asks about the old fracture, give the details above and emphasise the ongoing stiffness and widened heel.
candidate_instructions: Setting: General practice. Anthony Barnes, 58, presents with several months of progressive right heel/hindfoot pain, worse on weight-bearing, with a history of a prior right ankle fracture. In 8 minutes: take a focused history, explain your most likely diagnosis and differential to the patient, and outline your initial investigation and management plan. The examiner will provide examination/ROM findings when asked.
examiner_instructions: This tests heel-pain reasoning with interpretation of provided findings, leading to post-traumatic osteoarthritis (subtalar/ankle) given the prior fracture and a widened heel. If asked, provide: reduced plantarflexion (~20 degrees) and reduced subtalar inversion (~20 degrees) with dorsiflexion ~20 degrees (normal), painful hindfoot movement, and a widened heel (malunited calcaneal/ankle fracture). Reward framing plantar fasciitis as the single most common cause of inferior heel pain (clinical diagnosis, imaging not routine), with tender fat pad and calcaneal/tarsal stress fracture as alternatives - the latter important given prior bony injury (positive squeeze test, night/rest pain, early X-ray may be normal, MRI confirms). Reward reasoning to post-traumatic OA of the subtalar joint as the lead diagnosis here, and naming weight-bearing ankle/foot X-ray as the key investigation (joint space narrowing, osteophytes, prior fracture deformity). Reward a management/counselling limb: paracetamol first-line then topical/oral NSAID per eTG, weight management, footwear/orthotics and podiatry, physiotherapy, and orthopaedic referral for refractory disease. Prompt: 'Given the prior fracture and widened heel, which joint and diagnosis do you favour?'

criteria: Characterises the heel/hindfoot pain (site, weight-bearing pattern, stiffness) and the prior ankle fracture history
Screens for plantar fasciitis features (first-step/inferior heel pain) and Achilles tendinopathy
Screens not-to-be-missed causes (calcaneal/tarsal stress fracture, DVT, malignancy, infection)
Favours post-traumatic osteoarthritis (subtalar/ankle) given prior fracture, stiffness and widened heel
Correctly interprets provided ROM (plantarflexion and inversion reduced; dorsiflexion 20 degrees is normal)
Gives a sensible differential led by plantar fasciitis for inferior heel pain with fat-pad and stress-fracture alternatives
Requests weight-bearing ankle/foot X-ray as the key test; reserves MRI/US for occult stress fracture or soft-tissue uncertainty
Management/counselling: paracetamol first-line then topical/oral NSAID per eTG, weight management, footwear/orthotics, podiatry and physiotherapy
Orthopaedic referral for refractory post-traumatic OA (fusion/arthroplasty discussion) and appropriate safety-netting
Explains the diagnosis and link to the old injury in lay terms
Addresses work concerns and checks understanding

red_flags: Calcaneal/tarsal stress fracture - weight-bearing pain with prior bony injury, positive squeeze test, night/rest pain (early X-ray may be normal; MRI confirms)
Constitutional features (fever, weight loss, night pain) suggesting infection or malignancy
Neurovascular compromise or non-healing wound in the foot (consider diabetes/peripheral arterial disease)
australian_guidelines: RACGP/eTG: plantar fasciitis is the most common cause of inferior heel pain and is a clinical diagnosis - imaging is not routinely required
eTG analgesia: paracetamol first-line for osteoarthritis pain, adding topical or oral NSAID if tolerated, with weight management, footwear/orthoses, podiatry and physiotherapy

Weight-bearing ankle/foot X-ray is the key investigation for suspected post-traumatic osteoarthritis (joint space narrowing, osteophytes, prior fracture deformity); reserve MRI/US for occult stress fracture or soft-tissue uncertainty
Refer to orthopaedics for refractory post-traumatic ankle/subtalar osteoarthritis (fusion/arthroplasty discussion)
learning_objectives: Take a focused heel-pain history and interpret provided range-of-motion findings correctly
Reason from a prior ankle fracture and a widened heel to post-traumatic subtalar osteoarthritis
Include calcaneal stress fracture as a not-to-be-missed cause in a patient with prior bony injury
Outline an Australian management plan for hindfoot osteoarthritis and appropriate imaging
key_points: Plantar fasciitis is the most common cause of inferior heel pain and is a clinical diagnosis - no routine imaging
A widened heel with prior fracture suggests malunion and subtalar post-traumatic osteoarthritis
Normal ankle ROM is roughly dorsiflexion 15-20 degrees and plantarflexion 40-50 degrees - dorsiflexion 20 degrees is normal
Add calcaneal/tarsal stress fracture to the differential when there is prior bony injury and weight-bearing pain
Management: paracetamol then NSAID per eTG, weight/footwear/orthotics, podiatry, physiotherapy, orthopaedic referral if refractory

citations.claim: Plantar fasciitis, Achilles tendinopathy and osteoarthritis are core probability diagnoses in the painful foot and ankle, supporting the 'top three' heel differentials and the OA endpoint.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.1659

citations.source: AMC Handbook of Clinical Assessment.pdf, p.22

citations.claim: Unilateral limb symptoms warrant systematic screening for vascular and serious (e.g. DVT/malignancy) causes, supporting the vascular and red-flag screen.
